title: Smallpox in Delhi
hookLine: he nurses the sick during an epidemic in Delhi and dies of it at eight, where Gurdwara Bangla Sahib stands

lines: A CITY WITH A SICKNESS LOOSE.
THE PEOPLE WHO WENT IN ANYWAY.
cards: Empty streets. Door handles nobody wants to touch. Families keeping their distance from their own grandparents.
And the people who went in anyway: nurses, cleaners, delivery drivers, neighbors carrying soup. In 1664, while the child Guru Har Krishan was staying in Delhi, an epidemic swept the city.
Tradition names it smallpox, and some accounts add cholera. People were dying in the lanes. The eighth Guru was about seven, a guest far from home.

teach.b: Tradition says the young Guru did not hide. He went among the sick of Delhi, Hindu and Muslim alike, comforting and tending them, and his followers with him.

The house where he stayed, Raja Jai Singh's bungalow, had a well, and tradition says the Guru blessed its water and gave it to the sick. People came in crowds. Then the child caught the disease himself.
Sikhs tell of his last days with great tenderness. Burning with fever, he stayed calm. His frightened followers asked who would lead them after him.
Tradition says the dying boy gave a short, puzzling answer: Baba Bakale. The Baba, the next Guru, is at Bakala, a village in Punjab. He said no more.
That riddle is tomorrow's story, and the day after's. He died in Delhi in 1664, not yet eight years old. Here is what a visitor to Delhi can still see.
The bungalow became Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, which still draws crowds.
Beside it lies a large pool, fed, tradition says, from that same well, and people still take its water home to the sick.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, gurdwaras in Delhi, Bangla Sahib among them, cooked and delivered meals to people who couldn't leave home.
A child's service in one epidemic, echoing in another, more than three hundred and fifty years later.

how: Visitors to Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi often take water from its pool home for the sick, and Sikhs remember Guru Har Krishan's care for the sick in the daily Ardas.

games.q: you're a young Guru, a guest in Delhi, and an epidemic is spreading through the city. what do you do?
o: leave for Punjab while you still can.
go among the sick and tend them.
stay indoors and pray for the city.
games.why: tradition says he went among the sick, Hindu and Muslim alike, caught the disease, and died before he turned eight.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is unwell right now, in body or in spirit: a friend in the hospital, a parent with a long illness, someone having a hard month. Hold them without trying to fix anything.
If you pray, you can pray for them; if you don't, just wish them ease, breath by breath.

wordCard.voice: Baba Bakale. The dying child Guru's riddle-answer about where to find the next Guru, at a village called Bakala in Punjab.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: the Baba is at Bakala, the dying Guru's words about who comes next.

carryVoice: Your line: he served the sick. A frightened city, and a child who went toward it. Seventy-three days in.
